Other CPU serving stacks for batch throu.topic: Other CPU serving stacks for batch throughput with Intel AMX (SGLang CPU, xFT, IPEX/IPEX-LLM, OpenVINO/OVMS, llamafile, ik_llama.cpp, CTranslate2, ORT GenAI, DeepSpeed, TGI, PowerInfer, T-MAC, bitnet.cpp, KTransformers, newcomers), plus diffusion LLMs (DiffusionGemma)
Other CPU serving stacks for batch throu.summary: The SGLang CPU backend is the only other stack that could plausibly match or beat vLLM W8A8 on this VM with this model. It has had AMX GDN kernels for Qwen3-Next since January 2026 (PR #12525, merged 2026-01-30), and its cookbook has Xeon recipes for Qwen3.5/3.6-27B in BF16 and FP8. With stock flags it crashes on hybrid models: it needs `--mamba-radix-cache-strategy no_buffer --disable-overlap-schedule` or `--disable-radix-cache` (fix PR #37705 is still open). Three other gaps are still open PRs: speculative decoding (MTP or DFlash) for hybrid GDN on CPU, the compressed-tensors W8A8 path (PR #41330) and INT4 (PR #41331). Expect a modest gain at best (about 0.85x to 1.3x vLLM). vLLM's CPU backend copies SGLang's CPU kernels (`csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels`, synced 2026-07-30, AMX GDN included), and since 2026-08-03 it sends INT8 W8A8 linears to SGLang's AMX int8 kernel every time. So vLLM 0.31.0 W8A8 very likely already runs the same GEMM and GDN kernels; only the framework differs, plus the BF16 and FP8 paths, where vLLM uses oneDNN and SGLang its own AMX kernels. Several stacks are dead or archived: Intel xFasterTransformer, IPEX (end of life March 2026), IPEX-LLM and TGI; DeepSpeed's CPU path depended on IPEX. CTranslate2, KTransformers (MoE only, needs a GPU), PowerInfer, T-MAC and bitnet.cpp don't fit a dense 27B hybrid on AMX. llamafile is now llama.cpp underneath. ik_llama.cpp runs Qwen3.8-27B with MTP and faster AVX-512 kernels but has no AMX. Community numbers (62 tok/s Q8_0 and 77 tok/s IQ4_XS prompt processing, pp512, on 18 Cascade Lake cores) put it far below vLLM's 198 tok/s prefill. OpenVINO added a PagedGatedDeltaNet op in April 2026 and fixed the fusion that creates it on 2026-09-30, so a nightly might fix E10's serial prefill. It is still unlikely to beat vLLM W8A8. ONNX Runtime 1.30 added CPU kernels for Qwen3.5, but nothing shows AMX-class prefill. Diffusion LLMs (DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B, released 2026-06-10, runs on the vLLM CPU backend) trade compute for memory bandwidth. That pays off at batch 1 on GPUs, but offline batch work on this compute-limited CPU is the wrong regime. Each output token needs about (256-token canvas / 15–20 tokens per step) × (3.85B-active forward pass + 2 vocab projections), roughly 140–180 GFLOP, against 54 GFLOP for Qwen3.8-27B decode and about 8 GFLOP for its own autoregressive twin, Gemma 4 26B-A4B. Diffusion quality is also lower: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6 and GPQA 73.2 vs 82.3. Bottom line: no stack is clearly better than vLLM for Qwen3.8-27B. Run one same-VM SGLang vs vLLM comparison (W8A8, plus BF16 and FP8 in case E16 rejects W8A8). The big savings come from changing the model, not the stack: the MoE backbone with about 4B active parameters, run autoregressively with large batches. A DiffusionGemma vs Gemma 4 26B-A4B twin test is the cheap way to confirm that diffusion doesn't help on CPU.

findings.claim: SGLang's CPU backend (Intel PyTorch team) is AMX-native: its own C++ kernels for BF16, INT8 and FP8 GEMMs, fused MoE, and AMX attention (`--attention-backend intel_amx`). The LMSYS blog reports 6–14x better time to first token and 2–4x better time per output token than llama.cpp on a dual Xeon 6980P (DeepSeek-R1 INT8, 13x / 2.5x). The validated models are W8A8 INT8 (RedHatAI Llama-3.x and QwQ-32B quantized.w8a8, loaded with `--quantization w8a8_int8`) and FP8 checkpoints. It needs AMX, so 4th-generation Xeon or newer. Prebuilt images use `-xeon` tags (e.g. `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.13-xeon`) or build from `xeon.Dockerfile`.
sources: https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2025-07-14-intel-xeon-optimization (2025-07-14; search snippets only, page blocked from sandbox)
findings.relevance: It is the only non-vLLM stack whose kernels target the same AMX units at a similar efficiency class. Its published wins are against llama.cpp, not vLLM.

findings.claim: SGLang CPU supports hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models. PR #12525 '[CPU] Optimize Qwen3-next model on CPU' (merged 2026-01-30) added CPU kernels for chunk_gated_delta_rule, fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update/fused_gdn_gating, causal conv1d, rmsnorm and the fused qkvzba split. The Qwen3.6 cookbook (PR #32959) has Xeon 'balanced' recipes for the 27B dense model in bf16 and fp8 (`--device cpu`, tp 3/6) and notes speculative decoding is unsupported on Xeon. Qwen3.5-9B with `--device cpu --attention-backend intel_amx` was served on a 128-core Xeon 6 in PR #37705.
findings.relevance: Our architecture (qwen3_5 dense hybrid, 48 GDN layers + 16 full-attention layers) is in scope for SGLang CPU, so E14 is feasible.

findings.claim: With stock flags, SGLang crashes on CPU for Qwen3.5-family models before loading weights: 'AssertionError: extra_buffer needs CUDA/MUSA/NPU/ROCm/XPU (FLA)'. Until PR #37705 merges (open since 2026-09-03), start with `--mamba-radix-cache-strategy no_buffer --disable-overlap-schedule` or `--disable-radix-cache`, and set `SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1`.
findings.relevance: Without these flags an E14 run fails at startup and burns VM time.

findings.claim: SGLang CPU gaps as of 2026-10-04, all open PRs: compressed-tensors W8A8 INT8 routing to the AMX kernel (#41330, opened 2026-09-26); FP8 compressed-tensors (#41329); GGUF Q4/Q8, AWQ/GPTQ and INT4 through the AMX INT4 kernel, asymmetric only (#41331); speculative decoding for hybrid GDN on CPU (MTP #35835, DFlash #36782 and #37851). The DFlash PR branch reports Qwen3.5-9B on Xeon 6 (TP4, 128 cores) at 94 output tok/s at concurrency 1, accept length 6.1.
findings.relevance: Loading the community W8A8 checkpoint (Avesed, compressed-tensors) may need `--quantization w8a8_int8` and may fail if the scales or ignored layers don't match. MTP, which gave llama.cpp 1.5x (E12), isn't available in released SGLang CPU.

findings.claim: vLLM's CPU backend copies SGLang's CPU kernels into `csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels/` (synced to SGLang main on 2026-07-30 in PR #50387, including AMX GDN dispatch and pooled-state chunk_gated_delta_rule_cpu). Since PR #50801 (merged 2026-08-03), INT8 W8A8 linears with symmetric weights and aligned shapes always use SGLang's AMX `int8_scaled_mm_with_quant`. On Llama-3.1-8B W8A8 that measured 385 vs 360 total tok/s against oneDNN (+7%). Unquantized BF16 linears still use oneDNN only.
findings.relevance: vLLM 0.31.0 (E09) most likely already runs SGLang's INT8 GEMM and GDN kernels, so SGLang's possible edge for W8A8 is framework overhead and fusion, not kernels. For BF16 and FP8, vLLM's oneDNN path and SGLang's own AMX kernels differ more.

findings.claim: vLLM CPU enabled Gated DeltaNet (Qwen 3.5/3.6) on 2026-05-07 as an 'initial enablement' with fusion/varlen follow-ups promised. It added block-FP8 W8A16 linear support for Intel CPUs on 2026-05-06 (PR #41186) and FP8 W8A8 linear/MoE on 2026-09-18 (PR #49942); the W8A8 kernel targets Diamond Rapids (DMR), which has AMX-FP8, unlike Granite Rapids. Qwen publishes an official Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8: fine-grained FP8 with block size 128, quality described as nearly identical to BF16.
findings.relevance: This gives an official, quality-safe 8-bit checkpoint (half the bytes of BF16 for decode, BF16 AMX compute for prefill) on vLLM and SGLang. It is the fallback if E16 shows the community W8A8 degrades accuracy.

findings.claim: Intel's own CPU stacks are retired. intel/xFasterTransformer is archived on GitHub with no Qwen3.5/GDN support. Intel Extension for PyTorch stopped development after 2.8, reached end of life by end of March 2026, and is archived, with features upstreamed to PyTorch. intel/ipex-llm is archived. huggingface/text-generation-inference is archived (its CPU path was IPEX-based), and DeepSpeed's CPU inference depended on IPEX.
findings.relevance: These are not worth any VM-hours for this model.

findings.claim: OpenVINO added a paged GDN path: PagedGatedDeltaNet core op (#35051, April 2026), CPU enablement (#35070, merged 2026-04-28), PagedGatedDeltaNetFusion (#35532), and an output-shape fix to that fusion merged 2026-09-30 (#38488), probably after 2026.4.1. OpenVINO 2026.4 lists support for Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 27B on CPU and MTP speculative decoding for Qwen3.5/3.6 in GenAI. OVMS 2026.3 notes better stability and performance for linear-attention models. No published Xeon throughput for these models.
findings.relevance: E10's serial prefill at 34 tok/s with 48 Loop ops may come from the fusion not firing. A nightly might fix batching, but a bare single-request prefill was only 83 tok/s with the INT4→BF16 IR, so beating vLLM W8A8's 198 tok/s is unlikely.

findings.claim: ik_llama.cpp is actively maintained and supports the qwen35 architecture (Qwen3.8-27B) with MTP. Since PR #2260 (merged 2026-08-06), hybrid models no longer give wrong output with -np > 1. It has no AMX path; feature request #437 has been open since May 2025. A community AVX-512-VNNI tuning on an 18-core Cascade Lake measured Qwen3.8-27B pp512 at 51→62 tok/s for Q8_0 and 61→77 tok/s for IQ4_XS, with tg about 3.6 and 6.2 tok/s.
findings.relevance: Prefill on 8 Granite Rapids cores would land around 40–70 tok/s, an improvement over mainline llama.cpp (21–30) but 3–5x below vLLM W8A8. It cannot win the 512/128 workload.

findings.claim: llamafile 0.10.x (March–August 2026) is a rebuilt core that tracks recent llama.cpp and runs Qwen3.5 27B, so it shares llama.cpp's ggml CPU kernels.
findings.relevance: No gain over llama.cpp; skip.

findings.claim: KTransformers (kt-kernel) has AMX MoE kernels (up to 21.3 TFLOPS sustained per Xeon socket, 3.9x PyTorch) but is built for hybrid CPU/GPU MoE inference with experts on the CPU, now integrated with SGLang. Its v0.6.3 model list is MoE models (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM-5, Qwen3-MoE/Next).
findings.relevance: Not applicable to a dense 27B on a GPU-less VM. Relevant only if we switch to an MoE model, and SGLang/vLLM CPU already include similar AMX MoE kernels.

findings.claim: ONNX Runtime 1.30 added a GatedDeltaNet operator, fused CPU LinearAttention kernels (AVX-512, NEON, SVE) and VarlenCausalConvWithState for continuous batching, and Azure AI Foundry lists an optimized Qwen3.5-2B for CPU. No Xeon throughput or AMX-prefill evidence for a 27B. CTranslate2 has no hybrid/GDN support, only standard decoders such as Qwen2/Qwen3.
findings.relevance: ORT GenAI is a long shot (27B export, INT4 MatMulNBits); CTranslate2 can't run the model.

findings.claim: PyTorch 2.8 with torchao (DA8W8, A16W4, DA8W4) lowers quantized GEMMs to Inductor AMX templates. Intel reports parity with or better than vLLM offline on Llama-3.1-8B on one Xeon node, but there is no continuous-batching server or fast GDN path for our model.
findings.relevance: Shows a DA8W4 kernel (INT8 AMX compute with INT4 weights) exists; that combination would help prefill and decode at once. No usable engine for Qwen3.8 yet.

findings.claim: PowerInfer needs ReLU-sparse models. T-MAC and bitnet.cpp are LUT-based low-bit kernels for edge CPUs (AVX2/NEON, no AMX) that only pay off for 1–2-bit models. The relevant new model is Ternary Bonsai 2 27B (PrismML): a ternary Qwen3.8-27B-based model, about 6 GB, claimed to keep 98.2% of the base model's aggregate benchmark score. ik_llama.cpp merged Prism ternary kernels (PQ2_0/PTQ1_0, R8 IQK) in September 2026.
findings.relevance: Ternary weights cut decode bandwidth about 4.5x versus INT8, but prefill stays compute-bound on AVX-512, so it loses on 512/128. It would only pay off for decode-heavy jobs.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma (Google, released 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is a discrete-diffusion LLM on the Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE backbone (25.2B total, 3.85B active). A causal encoder reads the prompt and a bidirectional decoder denoises a 256-token canvas over up to 48 steps, keeping confident tokens through entropy-bound acceptance, with self-conditioning through the 262k-vocab embedding table. It makes about 15–20 tokens per forward pass. On one H100 at concurrency 1 it reaches 375 vs 199 tok/s output (1.9x) and 1,282 vs 205 tok/s per request, but its time to first token is 489 vs 53 ms. vLLM recipes cap max-num-seqs at 4 because state buffers scale with max_seqs × canvas × vocab. Quality is below the AR twin: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA Diamond 73.2 vs 82.3.
findings.relevance: The model the user asked about. Its speedup is a low-batch latency win bought with extra compute, and compute is the scarce resource on an 8-core AMX VM running offline batches. (Pages blocked from the sandbox; figures from search snippets.)

findings.claim: Independent evaluation finds autoregressive models give the highest throughput at every tested batch size, with block diffusion next and pure diffusion LMs slowest. Diffusion throughput stays flat as batch grows (compute-bound), and parallel decoding and dual cache help mainly at small batch. On CPU the per-output-token compute of DiffusionGemma is roughly (256 / 15–20) × (2 × 3.85B + 2 vocab projections of about 1.5 GFLOP each) ≈ 140–180 GFLOP. That compares with 54 GFLOP for Qwen3.8-27B decode and about 8 GFLOP for AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B.
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.23278 (FOCUS: dLLM decoding is compute-bound, most compute wasted on non-decodable tokens)
findings.relevance: At vLLM-CPU-class 7–10 TFLOPS effective, DiffusionGemma decode would top out around 40–70 output tok/s per VM whatever the batch, while its AR twin keeps scaling with batch. For offline 512/128 jobs, the MoE backbone matters, not diffusion.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma runs on vLLM's CPU backend. PR #59829 tested BF16 google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it on a 22-vCPU Xeon 8481C, using the default sync scheduling on CPU; async scheduling corrupted outputs before that fix. llama.cpp needs unmerged PR #24423 (llama-diffusion-cli) and Ollama doesn't support it. The SGLang dLLM path supports DiffusionGemma on GPUs (CPU unverified), and Gemma 4 itself runs on SGLang Xeon since PR #22498 (merged 2026-08-17).
findings.relevance: A diffusion-vs-AR twin test fits in our existing vLLM CPU Docker workflow; no new stack needed.

ideas.idea: E14: same-VM head-to-head of the SGLang CPU backend and vLLM CPU on Qwen3.8-27B. W8A8 (Avesed checkpoint with `--quantization w8a8_int8`), BF16, and the official Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8; `sglang.bench_offline_throughput` with random 512/128, 512/1 and 32/256 at 16 and 64 prompts. Flags: `--device cpu --attention-backend intel_amx --disable-radix-cache --disable-overlap-schedule`, `SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1`, `SGLANG_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND` set to the 8 physical cores, then 16 threads. Also run a 5-minute vLLM W8A8 512/128 ×16 reference on the same VM, and check output coherence on the three fixed prompts.
ideas.hypothesis: Both stacks share SGLang's AMX INT8 and GDN kernels, so SGLang W8A8 lands at 0.85–1.3x vLLM's 102 total tok/s on 512/128 ×16. In BF16 and FP8, where vLLM uses oneDNN and SGLang its own AMX kernels, SGLang is ≥1.15x faster. Falsified if SGLang W8A8 is below 0.9x and BF16 is within ±10%.
ideas.expected_gain: W8A8 blended $4.56/M → $3.5–5.4/M (×1/1.3 to ×1/0.85); a +15% result gives about $3.97/M (−$0.59/M). If E16 rejects W8A8, the fallback improves from vLLM BF16 at $7.45/M to SGLang FP8/BF16 at maybe $5–6.5/M.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 2.5–3 VM-hours on one E16ds_v7 (about $4–5): Docker pull of the `-xeon` image from Docker Hub on the VM (blocked only from the sandbox), about 60 GB of model downloads at about 1 GB/s, roughly 6 benchmark runs plus a vLLM reference. Risks: startup crash without the mamba flags; Avesed compressed-tensors scales not accepted by w8a8_int8 (PR #41330 unmerged), in which case use FP8/BF16 only; the newest `-xeon` tag may predate Qwen3.5 support, in which case build `xeon.Dockerfile` from main (+20–30 min).
ideas.prerequisites: New `bench/sglang_setup.sh` and `bench/sglang_bench.sh` chain that saves results after each step; pick the SGLang `-xeon` image tag on the VM; confirm the vLLM version and whether the `VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL` env var still exists (PR #50801 removed it, which tells whether 0.31.0 already uses the SGLang INT8 kernel).

ideas.idea: AR vs diffusion twin on vLLM CPU: Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it (AR) against DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B-it, same VM and same backbone, BF16 (FP8 if available). Workload 512/128 at concurrency 1, 4, 16 and 64 (DiffusionGemma with canvas_length 128 and 256), plus a 100-question GSM8K/MMLU-Pro subset for both and Qwen3.8-27B W8A8 as the quality reference. This extends R04.
ideas.hypothesis: DiffusionGemma beats its AR twin only at concurrency ≤4 and plateaus around 40–80 output tok/s because it is compute-bound. AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B at concurrency 64 is ≥2x DiffusionGemma's blended throughput, and both beat Qwen3.8-27B W8A8 on $/M because of 3.85B active parameters. Falsified if DiffusionGemma's blended tok/s at concurrency 16 is at least the AR twin's.
ideas.expected_gain: Rough compute and bandwidth model, assuming 3.5–7 TFLOPS effective for the MoE: AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B ≈ 0.56–1.1 s prefill + about 1 s decode share per request at batch 64 → 300–400 tok/s → $1.2–1.6/M (about $0.9–1.3/M with 8-bit experts). DiffusionGemma ≈ 24 TFLOP per 512/128 request → 3.5–7 s → 90–180 tok/s → $2.6–5.1/M. Either is a 1–4x cut against $4.56/M if quality is acceptable.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 2.5–3.5 VM-hours (about $4–6): two 50 GB downloads and a quality subset. Risks: DiffusionGemma CPU path is new (fixed only in sync mode; PR #59829 still open); diffusion state buffers are about 268 MB per sequence at canvas 256, fine on 128 GiB; vLLM CPU fused-MoE efficiency for Gemma 4 (GELU MoE) is unknown.
ideas.prerequisites: vLLM CPU image that includes DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4 (check `vllm --version` ≥ the June 2026 support); HF access from the VM for google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it (license acceptance may be needed); a quality bar from E16 to judge the model switch.

ideas.idea: Official Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 on vLLM CPU (block-FP8 W8A16 kernel, PR #41186) as a quality-safe 8-bit alternative to the community W8A8. Run 512/128 at 16 and 64 prompts on the same VM as a W8A8 reference; fold it into E14 if SGLang runs FP8 too.
ideas.hypothesis: FP8 W8A16 decodes at about W8A8 speed (same 27 GB of weights per step) and prefills at about BF16 speed (≈133 tok/s, or ≈110 with dequant overhead), so blended cost is about $5.3–6/M. That beats BF16's $7.45/M without E16's quantization risk; W8A8 stays cheaper if E16 passes.
ideas.expected_gain: Only if E16 rejects W8A8: fallback $7.45/M → about $5.5/M (−26%). Otherwise none, apart from insurance on quality.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 1 VM-hour (about $1.7): 28 GB download and 2–3 runs. Low risk: the kernel has been merged since May 2026 and lives in the vendored sgl-kernels.
ideas.prerequisites: E16 result; a vLLM image with PR #41186 (any build since mid-2026).

ideas.idea: OpenVINO GenAI nightly or the next release (with PagedGatedDeltaNetFusion fix #38488) plus an NNCF full-INT8 (weights and activations) IR. Re-run E10's prefill batch scaling (1/4/16 × 512/1) and confirm whether TTFT is still serial.
ideas.hypothesis: If the paged GDN fusion now fires, prefill scales with batch to ≥100 tok/s, and INT8 AMX brings it to 150–200 tok/s. Still ≤1x vLLM W8A8 on 512/128. Falsified (in OpenVINO's favour) if blended throughput beats 102 tok/s.
ideas.expected_gain: Low probability (<20%) of beating $4.56/M; the realistic outcome moves OpenVINO from $19–34/M to about $8–12/M.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 2 VM-hours (about $3.4), plus an NNCF INT8 export of 27B on the VM (~1 h, needs ≥64 GB RAM, and HF/pip access from the VM).
ideas.prerequisites: Release notes or a nightly that mentions hybrid-model batched prefill; otherwise skip.

ideas.idea: ik_llama.cpp refresh of the llama.cpp row: Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0_R8 and IQ4_XS, llama-batched-bench at np 1/16/32 plus a 512/128 server run with MTP; check output for hybrid multi-sequence correctness (PR #2260). Optionally add Ternary Bonsai 2 27B for a decode-heavy (32/256) workload.
ideas.hypothesis: Prefill on 8 Granite Rapids cores is 40–70 tok/s (1.5–2.5x mainline llama.cpp's 21–30, still about 3x below vLLM W8A8). Ternary Bonsai decode is ≥2x Q4_K_M decode at batch 16 but its prefill isn't faster.
ideas.expected_gain: No improvement on the best $/M for 512/128 (expected about $10–15/M against $4.56/M). It might win only decode-heavy jobs.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 1–1.5 VM-hours (about $2–2.5); GGUF downloads; no AMX path to debug.
ideas.prerequisites: Only worth running if a decode-heavy workload is added to scope; otherwise just record the literature numbers.

ideas.idea: Watch items, not tests yet: re-test SGLang CPU once (a) MTP or DFlash for hybrid GDN on CPU merges (#35835, #36782, #37851), (b) INT4/AWQ AMX routing merges (#41331), or (c) a DA8W4 (INT8-activation, INT4-weight AMX) linear path reaches vLLM or SGLang for dense models.
ideas.hypothesis: MTP gave 1.5x single-sequence decode in llama.cpp (E12). On SGLang CPU with batch 16–64 it would give +10–30% decode. DA8W4 would cut decode bytes in half while keeping INT8 AMX prefill.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode is about 50% of 512/128 wall time on vLLM W8A8 (mixed 100 s vs prefill-only 41 s at 16 prompts). +30% decode gives about −13% blended, $4.56 → about $4.0/M. DA8W4 could add another −15–25%.

Ollama for offline batch inference of Qw.topic: Ollama for offline batch inference of Qwen3.8-27B on Azure Xeon 6 (E16ds_v7), plus diffusion LLMs (DiffusionGemma and related) as requested by the user
Ollama for offline batch inference of Qw.summary: Ollama can't beat vLLM W8A8's $4.56/M on this VM, and it can't even match llama.cpp's batched $19-24/M. Since v0.30.0 (2026-06-01), Ollama on Linux has no engine of its own. It starts upstream llama.cpp `llama-server`, pinned to b11232 (2026-09-28), so we would get the same ggml kernels we already measured. Its Linux CPU build includes ggml's `sapphirerapids` variant (AMX_TILE and AMX_INT8), so on Granite Rapids it uses AMX automatically, which is the path that ran at about 3% of AMX peak in E07. Batching is llama-server's continuous batching with `-np = OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`, which defaults to 1. More importantly, Ollama's scheduler hard-codes `num_parallel=1` for the qwen35/qwen35moe/qwen3next architectures, and Qwen3.8 belongs to the qwen35 family. That limit is in every release from v0.30.0 to v0.35.1 and on main as of 2026-10-02, so Qwen3.8-27B requests are served one at a time. Expected cost is about $37/M (E03, one sequence, Q4_K_M with AMX), about $28/M if the MTP head Ollama turns on automatically is present, and about $26/M with num_thread=16. That is 6-8x vLLM and 1.1-1.9x llama.cpp batched. Patching the limit out only turns it into llama.cpp again, and its AMX path would corrupt multi-sequence decoding unless the AMX library were removed. On diffusion: DiffusionGemma (released 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0, 25.2B-total/3.8B-active MoE, 256-token canvas) has a vLLM recipe marked verified on Xeon 6 using the CPU backend with AMX-BF16. Neither Ollama nor mainline llama.cpp can run it; its llama.cpp PR is still unmerged on master as of 2026-10-04. Google and vLLM say its speed advantage holds at low concurrency, where decoding is memory-bound, and fades as the batch grows: on an H100, autoregressive serving catches up beyond about 32 concurrent users. On this CPU, which has far fewer usable FLOPs per byte of bandwidth, I estimate the crossover at about 8-16 sequences. For offline batch work it should therefore lose to its own autoregressive twin, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, which also scores 5-9 points higher on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. Both score well below Qwen3.8-27B on GPQA (73/82 vs about 89). Bottom line: close R07 (Ollama) on this desk evidence, or with a 20-minute smoke test at most. The diffusion-related idea most likely to pay off without changing models is DFlash2, a block-diffusion draft model for Qwen3.8-27B used in vLLM speculative decoding. If switching models is allowed, an autoregressive MoE with about 4B active parameters is a bigger lever than diffusion.

findings.claim: Ollama dropped its own Go/ggml engine. Commit 9db4bdb (#16031, 2026-05-29), 'runner: Remove CGO engines, use llama-server exclusively for GGML models', removed the vendored ggml/llama.cpp, the CGO runner and the Go model code. The first release with the change is v0.30.0 (2026-06-01). On Linux and Windows every GGUF model now runs in an upstream llama.cpp `llama-server` subprocess, built from the source pinned in LLAMA_CPP_VERSION (b11232, llama.cpp commit 6f767fe, 2026-09-28) plus small compatibility patches. The MLX engine is built for Metal only (Apple).
findings.relevance: For Qwen3.8 on x86, Ollama is llama-server with Ollama's defaults. Its best case is bounded by our llama.cpp measurements (E03/E05/E12), and it inherits llama.cpp's ~3%-of-AMX-peak prefill.

findings.claim: Ollama uses Intel AMX automatically. The Linux CPU build uses the `cpu` preset (GGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS=ON, GGML_BACKEND_DL=ON, GGML_NATIVE=OFF) with gcc-toolset-13. In llama.cpp b11232 that builds a `sapphirerapids` ggml-cpu variant with AVX512_BF16, AMX_TILE and AMX_INT8, and ggml loads the highest-scoring variant at run time. The AMX path covers quantized types only (AMX-INT8). There is no AMX-BF16 GEMM path for BF16 weights.
findings.relevance: Ollama brings no AMX advantage over our llama.cpp builds. It runs the same AMX kernel E07 measured at ~3% of peak, and the one E04 found corrupts multi-sequence decoding for Qwen3.5-family models.

findings.claim: Ollama never serves Qwen3.8 requests in parallel. server/sched.go forces numParallel=1, with the warning 'model architecture does not currently support parallel requests', for mllama, qwen3vl, qwen3vlmoe, qwen35, qwen35moe, qwen3next, lfm2, lfm2moe and nemotron_h*. This holds whatever OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL is set to. The list is the same in v0.30.0, v0.35.1 (2026-10-01) and main 42e911b (2026-10-02). Commit e36f389 (#14103, 2026-02-05) first added qwen3next/lfm under the old engine. Users report it in issues #14510 ('ollama 0.17.4+ qwen3.5 35b/27b only have 1 active request'), #14879 and #14621, and a third-party fork exists only to lift it.
findings.relevance: This is the decisive fact. With one sequence at a time, decode stays memory-bound at ~4 tok/s, and aggregate throughput can't rise the 4-5x that batching gave llama.cpp (E05) or the gains it gave vLLM.

findings.claim: Qwen3.8 is the qwen35 architecture family in Ollama. create/metadata.go maps the HF 'qwen3_5' architecture to the qwen35 family and picks the 'qwen3.8' renderer from the chat template. Qwen3.8 support needs Ollama 0.32.12 or later. The library tag qwen3.8:27b is an 18 GB Q4_K_M with a 931 MB vision encoder; Q8_0 (30 GB) and BF16 tags also exist. Ollama automatically passes `--mmproj` for qwen35 GGUFs that contain vision tensors.
findings.relevance: Confirms that the parallel=1 limit applies to our exact model.

findings.claim: How Ollama launches and batches. It runs `llama-server -c NumCtx*numParallel -np numParallel` and keeps llama-server's continuous batching (cont_batching=true by default, per-slot context, kv_unified=false). An Ollama-side semaphore admits numParallel requests, and up to OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE=512 more wait in a queue. Defaults: OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1 (since #11330, 2025-07); num_batch 512 (passed as -b/-ub); num_thread 0, which leaves llama-server's default of physical cores (8 on E16ds_v7); num_ctx 4096 when no GPU VRAM is found. If the GGUF has nextn/MTP tensors, Ollama adds `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 4` automatically. The DFlash external-draft type is also wired in.
sources: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b11232/common/common.cpp (common_cpu_get_num_math returns physical cores on x86 Linux)
findings.relevance: Ollama's default 8 threads leaves E08's +14-25% prefill gain from 16 threads unused (it can be set with num_thread). MTP may be on by default, which helps single-sequence decode by about 1.5x (E12).

findings.claim: Estimated Ollama cost on E16ds_v7 for the 512+128 workload, computed from our own measurements with Ollama forced to one sequence. Q4_K_M AMX at 8 threads: prefill 28.7 tok/s, decode 3.88 tok/s (E03), so 50.8 s per request = $37.1/M. With the automatic MTP head (E12: 1.55x decode, i.e. 6.0 tok/s): 39.2 s = $28.6/M. Adding num_thread=16 (+14-25% prefill, E08): about $26-27/M. That is 5.7-8.1x vLLM W8A8 ($4.56/M) and 1.1-1.9x llama.cpp batched ($19.3-23.9/M).
findings.relevance: Answers the bottom-line question: Ollama is at best equal to llama.cpp single-sequence and worse than llama.cpp batched. Medium confidence because whether the library tag carries the MTP head was not verified.

findings.claim: Workarounds can't beat llama.cpp. Running several Ollama instances (each loading its own 17.4 GB copy) doesn't help: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound at ~100 GB/s, so N copies share about the same ~5 tok/s total, and prefill shares the same cores. Patching out the qwen35 parallel limit just gives llama-server -np N. With Ollama's AMX variant loaded, that would produce wrong multi-sequence output (E04) unless libggml-cpu-sapphirerapids is deleted so a non-AMX variant loads, which is llama.cpp no-AMX batched ($19-24/M) plus Ollama overhead.
findings.relevance: Confirms the expectation that Ollama is 'at best equal to llama.cpp' on this architecture and CPU.

findings.claim: Published Ollama vs vLLM and llama.cpp comparisons all come from GPUs and favor vLLM heavily. Red Hat (A100-40GB, Llama-3.1-8B FP16, GuideLLM, 2025-08): vLLM peaked at 793 tok/s vs 41 tok/s for Ollama with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=32 (P99 TTFT 80 ms vs 673 ms). Other 2026 write-ups report 2.3-2.8x at 8-16 concurrent requests on H100 and about 8x at batch 64 (Llama 3.3 70B). llama.cpp is quoted as 15-30% faster than Ollama. After v0.30 there are reports of regressions: #16415 (much slower than v0.24 on multiple Pascal GPUs) and #18038 (llama-server high CPU use while generating). I found no CPU or Xeon benchmark of Ollama against vLLM.
findings.relevance: Independent results agree with the code reading: Ollama trades throughput for ease of use. The numbers are older and GPU-only, so they serve only as supporting evidence.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma (Google DeepMind, 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is a block-diffusion MoE built on the Gemma 4 26B-A4B backbone: 25.2B total and about 3.8-4B active parameters, 128 experts with top-8 routing, 256K context. It denoises a 256-token canvas, up to 48 steps per block, with an entropy-bound sampler that fixes about 15-20 tokens per forward pass, then commits the block to the KV cache. vLLM supports it natively (min 0.24.0), and the vLLM recipe marks Xeon 6 as 'verified' with the CPU image vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:latest-x86_64 in BF16 using AMX. The recipe sets --max-num-seqs 4 on GPU because the sampler state is max_seqs x canvas x 262k vocab in fp32. That is about 0.27 GB per sequence, so a 128 GiB CPU VM can run 16-32 sequences.
findings.relevance: The user asked about diffusion models. DiffusionGemma is the one diffusion LLM with a supported, verified CPU (Xeon 6, AMX) path in a stack we already run (vLLM CPU).

findings.claim: Ollama and mainline llama.cpp can't run DiffusionGemma. llama.cpp master 7f2dd88 (2026-10-04) treats only DREAM, LLADA, LLADA_MOE and RND1 as diffusion architectures, served through `llama-diffusion-cli` only, not llama-server. DiffusionGemma support is in unmerged PR #24423/#24427, where a maintainer prefers a general diffusion server. Ollama reports 'unknown model architecture: diffusion-gemma'. LLaDA2.x GGUFs don't run in llama.cpp either; a separate 'diffuse-cpp' CPU engine exists for LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B.
findings.relevance: A diffusion test would have to use vLLM CPU, not Ollama or llama.cpp.

findings.claim: Diffusion's advantage shrinks with batch size. vLLM recipe, single H100, concurrency 1: output 375 vs 199 tok/s (1.9x) against autoregressive Gemma 4 26B-A4B, with TTFT about 10x higher. Google's overview and secondary sources: 'the throughput advantage fades at higher batch sizes'; diffusion wins up to about 32 concurrent users, after which autoregressive serving catches up because each canvas position costs extra compute. One real test of LLaDA-8B on a MacBook CPU/GPU gave 1.05 tok/s vs 29.7 tok/s autoregressive.
findings.relevance: Our workload is offline batch, the regime where diffusion's advantage disappears. CPUs reach the compute-bound regime at a smaller batch than GPUs.

findings.claim: Estimate (mine) of DiffusionGemma vs autoregressive on E16ds_v7. One denoising step over a 256-token canvas costs about 256 x 2 x 3.8e9 = 1.95 TFLOP per sequence. A 128-token answer needs about 7-17 steps, so 14-33 TFLOP, against about 1 TFLOP autoregressive: 14-34x more compute per output token. At the 3.5-7 TFLOPS effective that vLLM CPU sustains (E09 BF16 prefill: 133 tok/s x 54 GFLOP = 7.2 TFLOPS dense), that is 2.6-10.5 s per request including prefill: 61-246 tok/s, or $1.9-7.7/M. Its autoregressive twin at batch 64 reads about 52 GB (BF16, all experts) per step, roughly 0.55 s, so 1.1 s of decode per request plus 0.55-1.1 s prefill: about $1.2-1.6/M (about $2.6/M at batch 16), and less with INT8 weights. The CPU crossover is about 8-16 sequences because effective FLOPs per byte here are around 50, against around 300 on an H100.
findings.relevance: Suggests DiffusionGemma lands in the same range as our current $4.56/M, and that the same-backbone autoregressive MoE is the better CPU candidate if switching models is acceptable. Untested: vLLM CPU fused-MoE efficiency and actual step counts are unknown.

findings.claim: Quality: DiffusionGemma scores below its autoregressive twin, and both score below Qwen3.8-27B. DiffusionGemma vs Gemma 4 26B-A4B: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA Diamond 73.2 vs 82.3; one source gives 69.1 for DiffusionGemma, reported as LiveCodeBench v6 against Gemma 4's 77.1, and another says AIME 2026 69.1 vs 88.3. Aggregators list Qwen3.8-27B at GPQA 89.2 and LiveCodeBench v6 90.3. vLLM's CI GSM8K threshold for the FP8 DiffusionGemma is 0.84 (5-shot), and the model has no per-request temperature or seed (fixed internal schedule).
findings.relevance: Switching to DiffusionGemma costs about 16 GPQA points against Qwen3.8-27B. Whether that is 'acceptable quality' depends on the task, and E16-style task accuracy would be required.

findings.claim: A diffusion technique that keeps our model: z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 is a block-diffusion draft model for speculative decoding of Qwen3.8-27B, with block 8 and acceptance length 4.1-5.5 vs a maximum of 8. On an H200 with SGLang at concurrency 1 it gives 3.43x (vs 2.59x for Qwen3.8's built-in MTP). At concurrency 32 the gain falls to 1.0-1.45x. SGLang support is stated; vLLM and llama.cpp support are claimed. This contradicts E12's note that no DFlash draft model exists for Qwen3.8, which is outdated or was missed.
findings.relevance: In vLLM CPU at 16 sequences, decode runs at only about 1.7 TFLOPS effective, well below the about 7-10 TFLOPS prefill reaches, so it isn't compute-bound and a high-acceptance drafter could still cut decode time. Decode is about 60% of the request time, so the cost could drop 10-20% without changing models or quality.

ideas.idea: Same-VM comparison of DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B (block diffusion) vs Gemma 4 26B-A4B (autoregressive twin) on vLLM CPU BF16, max-num-seqs 1/4/8/16/32, 512-in/128-out, canvas_length 256 vs 128, plus a quick GSM8K/MMLU-Pro subset for quality
ideas.hypothesis: DiffusionGemma beats its autoregressive twin on aggregate tok/s only at 1-4 sequences (at most about 1.5x) and loses from about 8-16 sequences. Its best offline $/M will be at least about $2/M (estimate $2-8/M), while the autoregressive MoE reaches about $1.2-2.6/M at 16-64 sequences, i.e. at least 2x cheaper than Qwen3.8 W8A8 at $4.56/M, but with lower GPQA (82 vs 89).
ideas.expected_gain: If switching models is acceptable: Gemma-4-26B-A4B autoregressive at about 300 tok/s gives 1.681/3600/300 x 1e6 = $1.56/M (-66% vs $4.56/M). DiffusionGemma at 61-246 tok/s gives $1.9-7.7/M (between -58% and +69%). For Qwen3.8-27B itself: none.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 2.5 VM-hours (~$4.2) on one E16ds_v7: two HF downloads of about 52 GB each (fine at ~1 GB/s from the VM), Docker image vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:latest-x86_64 pulled on the VM (hub.docker.com is blocked only from the sandbox). Risks: the CPU diffusion path is new (vLLM issue #59828 reports a CPU async-output buffer-aliasing bug), fused-MoE CPU efficiency is unknown, per-request temperature is unsupported, and the recipe's max-num-seqs 4 needs raising on CPU (0.27 GB of sampler state per sequence).

ideas.hypothesis: Decode in vLLM CPU at 16 sequences isn't compute-bound (about 1.7 TFLOPS effective vs about 7-10 TFLOPS in prefill), so a drafter with acceptance length 4-5.5 raises aggregate decode 1.2-1.5x at 16 sequences and 1.0-1.2x at 32 sequences, with identical greedy text up to numerical ties.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 1-1.5 VM-hours once E17's vLLM build is up. Main blocker: whether the vLLM CPU backend accepts the dflash speculative method (unknown; MTP itself is being tested in E17). Drafter download from HF on the VM.

ideas.expected_gain: None expected: it confirms a negative. Predicted from E03/E12: 512/28.7 + 128/6.0 = 39.2 s per request, $28.6/M.

open_questions: Does Ollama's qwen3.8:27b library tag include the blk.64 nextn/MTP tensors, so that MTP (draft 4) is on by default, or is MTP a separate tag? This moves the Ollama estimate between about $28/M and $37/M.

What is Ollama's actual reason for forcing parallel=1 on qwen35/qwen3next? The code only cites the generic issue #4165. Is it recurrent-state memory accounting, a correctness bug (possibly related to the llama.cpp AMX multi-sequence corruption in E04), or MTP/checkpoint interaction? Is a fix planned?

How efficient is vLLM CPU's fused-MoE kernel for 128-expert top-8 Gemma 4 layers at 256xB tokens per step? This decides whether DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4 26B-A4B reach the 3.5-7 TFLOPS assumed in the estimate.

How many denoising steps does DiffusionGemma need for a 128-token answer with entropy_bound 0.1, and does canvas_length 128 (supported per request through diffusion_canvas_length) cut compute about 2x without hurting quality?
Does the vLLM CPU backend support the DFlash/DFlash2 speculative method for Qwen3.8 (hybrid Gated DeltaNet state rollback on rejection)?

Is a switch from Qwen3.8-27B to a weaker ~4B-active MoE (Gemma 4 26B-A4B autoregressive or DiffusionGemma, about 7-16 GPQA points lower) within the project's 'acceptable quality' bar? Only the orchestrator or user can decide, and E16-style task accuracy would be needed.

Models better suited than dense Qwen3.8-.topic: Models better suited than dense Qwen3.8-27B to CPU batch inference on E16ds_v7 (small dense, low-active MoE, hybrid, and diffusion LMs such as DiffusionGemma)
Models better suited than dense Qwen3.8-.summary: The E17 runs that have finished change the picture. Qwen3.8-27B W8A8 at 64 prompts costs $3.47/M blended (134 tok/s), and its decode step fits t(n) ≈ 0.29 s + 13 ms × n. At n=64 the per-sequence term (0.83 s) is about 3× the weight-read term, and prefill takes about half of each 512/128 request. So the cost is set by ACTIVE-parameter FLOPs, not by weight bandwidth, and the lever is fewer active params. Total params matter only for the 128 GiB limit and a ~0.3 s weight read per step. No Qwen3.8 model sits between the 27B and Flash-Next (176B in all, 6B active, does not fit in 128 GiB, no mainline CPU support). The best candidate is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: Apache-2.0, April 2026, the same Gated DeltaNet hybrid family and tokenizer, 3B active (~4.8 vs ~54 GFLOP/token), MMLU-Pro 85.2 and GPQA 86.0 vs Qwen3.8-27B's ~84-86 and 89.2, and vLLM lists Xeon 6 BF16 serving for its Qwen3.5 twin. I estimate $0.76-1.11/M at INT8 with 128 prompts and $1.2-1.7/M at BF16, 2-4× cheaper than today. The dense control is Qwen3.5-9B (MMLU-Pro 82.5, GPQA 81.7, IFEval 91.5; ~$1.0-1.2/M INT8, ~$1.4-1.8/M BF16). It has the lowest technical risk because it runs exactly the code path already working for the 27B. Gemma 4 26B-A4B costs about the same but scores lower (82.6/82.3), so it is a hedge. Phi-4 is dominated: Dec-2024, MMLU-Pro 70.4, GPQA 56.1, IFEval 63, 16k context, ~$1.7/M because 14B dense, and I found no primary source for a "Phi-5". gpt-oss-20b, Nemotron 3 Nano, Granite 4.x, LFM2 and Mistral Small 4 lose on quality, add reasoning tokens, or are too big. DiffusionGemma (Gemma-4-26B-A4B converted to 256-token block diffusion) buys fewer weight loads with ~25× more FLOPs per generated token. That helps batch-1 latency on GPUs, but on a FLOP-poor CPU that already batches 64-256 requests I estimate it costs 2-3.5× more than autoregressive Gemma 4 ($1.4-3.1/M) and it scores lower (MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA 73.2 vs 82.3), so I don't recommend it beyond an optional sanity check. The quality risk for extraction, classification and summarization is mainly instruction and format adherence in non-thinking mode, because all the published scores are thinking-mode. Gate any switch with the E16 harness plus IFEval and a JSON-extraction set. Bottom line: benchmark Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (P0, BF16 then FP8/INT8) and Qwen3.5-9B (P0 dense control) on vLLM CPU at 64-256 prompts, add Gemma 4 26B-A4B as a P2 hedge, and run DiffusionGemma at most as a P3 curiosity. Note: WebFetch was blocked for nearly every host (qwen.ai, huggingface, arxiv, vllm, lmsys, intel, google), so third-party facts come from search-result snippets, and the cost numbers are my own scaling estimates calibrated on E17 (in the scratchpad: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-az-slm/009ea70f-3087-589b-9bcd-b220bdd76de5/scratchpad/est.py).

findings.claim: Calibration from our own data (E17, vLLM 0.31.0 CPU, Qwen3.8-27B W8A8, E16ds_v7, 8 threads). Mixed 512/128 gives 86.8 tok/s at n=16, 116.1 at n=32 and 134.4 at n=64, so n=64 costs 1.681/(134.4×3600)×1e6 = $3.47/M, better than the $4.56/M from E09 at n=16. Prefill is flat at 165-196 tok/s, i.e. 5.09 ms/token for ~54 GFLOP, which is 0.094 ms/GFLOP. Decode wall time for 256 steps is 151.8 s at n=16, 185.5 s at n=32 and 296.8 s at n=64. After removing the 32-token prefill this fits t(n) ≈ 0.29 s + 13 ms × n. The 0.29 s matches reading ~28 GB of INT8 weights at ~97 GB/s. The 13 ms per sequence is ~1.5-3 ms of GDN recurrent state traffic (48 layers × 48 heads × 128×128 × 4 B ≈ 151 MB per sequence if the state is fp32) plus ~10 ms of compute for ~56.5 GFLOP (0.175 ms/GFLOP). The same model predicts $3.54/M at n=64, against $3.47/M measured. W4A16 prefill runs at only 32 tok/s, 16 threads halve throughput (66 vs 134 tok/s), and MTP lowers throughput.
findings.relevance: At realistic batch sizes, dense 27B decode is dominated by per-sequence compute and state, not weight bandwidth. A 512/128 request costs 512×5.09 ms + 128×(0.29/n + 0.013) s, which tends to a floor of about $3.1/M however large the batch. Cutting active params (FLOPs) is the only big lever. INT4 on vLLM CPU is a dead end.

findings.claim: The Qwen3.8 open-weight lineup is 27B dense, Flash-Next (125B main + 51B n-gram embedding + 4B MTP head, 6B active, 512 experts with top-10 + 1 shared, released 2026-08-26) and 2.4T-A95B. No Qwen3.8 model exists between 27B and Flash-Next, and a Qwen3.8-35B-A3B is only a community request. Flash-Next scores GPQA Diamond 91.7 vs 89.2 for the 27B. Mainline llama.cpp does not support it (Unsloth GGUFs need an unmerged PR), and vLLM support is PR #53896, GPU-focused.
findings.relevance: The cheaper Qwen options are earlier-generation models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B). Flash-Next has ~176B params, so even at 4-bit it does not fit in 128 GiB. A Standard_E20ds_v7 (20 vCPU, 160 GiB, $2.079/h Linux in eastus2 per the Retail Prices API, the same per-core price as E16ds_v7) could hold a 4-bit build if CPU support lands.

findings.claim: Qwen3.8-27B quality: GPQA Diamond 89.2 (model card) and IFBench 79.5 vs 69.1 for Qwen3.6-27B. Third-party MMLU-Pro runs give 84.3-85.5. Qwen3.6-27B scored MMLU-Pro 86.2 and GPQA 87.8. The published numbers are thinking mode.
findings.relevance: This is the quality bar. The largest gain from 3.6 to 3.8 is in instruction following (+10 IFBench), which is the capability that matters most for strict-format extraction.

findings.claim: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was released 2026-04-15 under Apache 2.0, with 35B total and ~3B active params. It has 40 layers as 10 × (3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated full attention), each followed by an MoE layer with 256 experts (8 routed + 1 shared, expert FFN 512). Hidden size is 2048, the GDN layers have 16 QK and 32 V heads of dim 128, the attention layers have 16 Q and 2 KV heads of dim 256, and native context is 262k. It supports thinking and non-thinking modes. MMLU-Pro is 85.2 and GPQA Diamond 86.0, against 86.2 and 87.8 for Qwen3.6-27B. Qwen3.6-27B wins 32 benchmarks, 35B-A3B wins 4 (mostly vision). An official FP8 checkpoint exists. My count from that config: ~32.2B expert params, ~2.4B non-embedding active params, so ~4.8 GFLOP/token in prefill (vs ~54) and GDN state of ~63 MB per sequence in fp32.
findings.relevance: This is the best quality per active parameter available. It uses the same architecture family, tokenizer and chat template as our 27B, so prompts and the GDN code path carry over. It has 11× fewer FLOPs per token, and at INT8 it fits easily (~36 GB of weights).

findings.claim: Qwen3.5 family, from the official tables (thinking mode). 27B: MMLU-Pro 86.1, GPQA 85.5, IFEval 95.0. 35B-A3B: 85.3, 84.2, 91.9. 122B-A10B: 86.7, 86.6, 93.4. 9B: 82.5, 81.7, 91.5 (LiveCodeBench v6 82.7). 4B: MMLU-Pro 79.1. The 9B is a dense hybrid of 8 × (3 GDN + 1 attention) and the small models (0.8B/2B/4B/9B) came out on 2026-03-02. All are Apache 2.0 and multimodal.
findings.relevance: Within one generation, the 3B-active MoE loses about 3 IFEval points to the 27B dense model, and the 9B dense loses about 3.5. This is the likely size of the instruction-following risk. The 122B-A10B does not fit at INT8 (~122 GB), and at INT4 it hits vLLM CPU's slow W4A16 path.

findings.claim: vLLM CPU support. The vLLM recipes list Intel Xeon 6 for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (BF16, vLLM ≥ 0.17), Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-8B/14B, Gemma 4 (vllm/vllm-openai-cpu image) and gpt-oss-20b. The CPU backend has an MoE path controlled by VLLM_CPU_MOE_PREPACK (on by default, IPEX GatedMLPMOE) and VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL (experimental AMX small-batch kernels that need BF16 weights and dimensions divisible by 32). It supports INT8 W8A8 per-channel/per-token MoE experts and FP8 W8A16 linear and MoE layers (FP8 W8A8 is a separate PR). vLLM issue #43326 reports Gemma 4 26B-A4B failing because the CPU fused-MoE path lacked GELU_TANH; later docs list gelu_tanh among the cpu_moe activations.
findings.relevance: The top MoE candidates should load on our existing vLLM 0.31 CPU image with no new stack. The main unknown is how efficient vLLM's CPU MoE prefill kernels are.

findings.claim: llm-compressor has no tested W8A8 recipe for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (issue #2787). Qwen3_5Moe is missing from the SmoothQuant/AWQ mapping tables, the fused 3D expert tensors must be split, and the GDN linears need handling. Community W8A8 and W8A16 builds exist (on ModelScope and from community uploaders), but their quality is unverified.
findings.relevance: Test the official BF16 weights first (quality-safe, ~70 GB, fits), then the official FP8 checkpoint (W8A16 on CPU) or a self-made round-to-nearest W8A8. Don't depend on an unverified community INT8 quant.

findings.claim: MoE batching caveat, quantified. Assuming uniform routing, the fraction of experts a decode step touches is f(n) = 1 − (1 − k/E)^n. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (k=8, E=256): 0.40 at n=16, 0.87 at n=64, 0.98 at n=128. Gemma 4 26B-A4B (8/128): 0.64, 0.98, 1.00. gpt-oss-20b (4/32): 0.88 at n=16. Nemotron 3 Nano (6/128): 0.95 at n=64. Batch-aware routing work (OEA, ICML 2026) confirms that MoE decode becomes memory-bound at moderate batch, with latency set by the number of activated experts. Re-routing to already-loaded experts cut MoE-layer decode latency by 39% for Qwen3-30B at batch 16.
findings.relevance: At our batch sizes, an MoE reads essentially ALL its expert weights every decode step: 35B-A3B at INT8 reads ~34 GB, i.e. ~0.35 s per step, more than the 27B's 0.29 s. So the MoE saving comes from compute (the per-sequence 13 ms drops to ~3.4 ms) and from prefill, not from bandwidth. INT4 MoE would only help bandwidth, and that is not the bottleneck.

findings.claim: Estimated throughput and $/M for the candidates on E16ds_v7 at $1.681/h, 512/128, vLLM continuous batching. Method: scale the E17 calibration by active FLOPs, with efficiency factors relative to dense 27B (dense 0.7-0.95; MoE prefill 0.35/0.5/0.7, MoE decode 0.4/0.5/0.7), BF16 compute ×1.47 (E09: 133 vs 198 tok/s), weight read = bytes × f(n)/97 GB/s, plus state/KV traffic. Per-request seconds s = 512·p + 128·t(n)/n, and $/M = 1.681·s/3600/640·1e6. Worked example, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B W8A8 at n=128 (mid): p = 0.094 × 4.8/0.5 = 0.90 ms (1105 tok/s prefill); b = 0.175 × 5.8/0.5 + 1.4 = 3.4 ms; a = (2.5 + 32.2 × 0.98)/97 = 0.35 s; t = 0.35 + 0.44 = 0.79 s (162 tok/s decode); s = 0.46 + 0.79 = 1.25 s, so 510 tok/s and $0.92/M. Results, pessimistic/mid/optimistic: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B W8A8 n=128 $1.11/$0.92/$0.76 (n=256 $0.98/$0.79/$0.64), BF16 n=128 $1.70/$1.42/$1.20, FP8-W8A16 n=128 $1.45/$1.16/$0.94. Qwen3.5-9B W8A8 n=128 $1.24/$1.05/$0.96, BF16 $1.80/$1.53/$1.39. Qwen3.5-4B W8A8 n=128 $0.79/$0.66/$0.60. Gemma 4 26B-A4B W8A8 n=128 $1.11/$0.89/$0.72, BF16 $1.69/$1.36/$1.11. Phi-4 14B W8A8 n=128 $1.92/$1.74/$1.67. gpt-oss-20b, MXFP4 dequantized to BF16, n=128 $1.65/$1.30/$1.02 before any reasoning-token overhead. Baseline Qwen3.8-27B W8A8: $3.54 modeled at n=64 vs $3.47 measured, with a floor of ~$3.1/M. Sensitivity: if MoE prefill efficiency is only 0.2 (or 0.1), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B W8A8 is still $1.47 (or $2.32)/M. Spot-equivalent is ×0.193, and E16ds_v6 (if E18 shows equal throughput) is ×0.79.
findings.relevance: This is the core expected-gain estimate: a 2-4.5× lower $/M than the current best ($3.47/M) for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B. MoE prefill efficiency on CPU is the largest uncertainty and is what the first test must measure.

findings.claim: Gemma 4 (April 2026, Apache 2.0) comes as E2B, E4B, 26B-A4B MoE and 31B dense. The 26B-A4B has 25.2B total and 3.8B active params, 30 layers (25 sliding-window 1024 + 5 global), hidden 2816, a dense GeGLU FFN of 2112 in parallel with 128 experts (top-8, FFN 704) plus a shared expert, a 262k vocab and 256k context. Thinking-mode scores: 31B has MMLU-Pro 85.2 and GPQA 84.3. The 26B-A4B has 82.6 and 82.3 (AIME 2026 88.3, LiveCodeBench v6 77.1). E4B has 69.4 and 58.6. llama.cpp supports Gemma 4.
findings.relevance: It costs about the same as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on CPU but scores ~2.6-3.7 points lower. It is a cross-family hedge, and it is the autoregressive twin of DiffusionGemma, so it serves as the control for any diffusion test.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma (Google DeepMind, 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is Gemma-4-26B-A4B (25.2B total, 3.8B active) converted to block discrete diffusion with <10% of the original training tokens. It denoises 256-token canvases with the entropy-bounded sampler (at most 48 steps, ~12 on average, ~20 tokens per forward on average; IFEval no-thinking uses 9.0 tokens per forward over 14.4 steps). Each step processes 256 positions and takes ~3.2× an autoregressive step on H100. At batch 1 on H100 it reaches 1456 tok/s vs 204 for AR Gemma 4 (303 with MTP), but AR regains the throughput lead at ~32 concurrent users. Quality vs Gemma 4 26B-A4B: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA Diamond 73.2 vs 82.3, also lower on AIME 2026, LiveCodeBench and tau2. IFEval is 94.5 no-thinking. Support: vLLM via Model Runner V2 ModelState hooks (GPU-oriented, CPU backend unverified), HF Transformers 5.11, MLX, and llama.cpp only through unmerged PR #24423/#24427 with a single-request llama-diffusion-cli (no batched server).
findings.relevance: This answers the user's question. Diffusion LMs swap memory round-trips for FLOPs: one 128-token answer costs 256 × K ≈ 3,000-3,700 token-forwards instead of 128 decode steps shared across the batch.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma on our CPU, estimated. With the per-position cost equal to Gemma 4 prefill (W8A8 mid: 0.094 × 5.4/0.5 = 1.02 ms), a request costs (512 + 256 × K) × p. At K=12 that is 3,584 × 1.02 ms = 3.65 s, or $2.66/M, against $0.89/M for AR Gemma 4 at n=128, about 3× worse. The range is $1.36/M (optimistic, K=8) to $3.12/M (K=14.4), and $3.9-4.6/M at BF16. The CPU ridge point is ~10.6 TFLOPS / 97 GB/s ≈ 110 FLOP/byte, versus ~300 on H100. So autoregressive batching saturates compute at a much smaller batch than on the GPU, and the batch where AR overtakes diffusion (≈32 on H100) is even lower here. The same reasoning applies to LLaDA2.x-mini, I-DLM and similar models.
findings.relevance: Diffusion models are the wrong direction for offline batch work on a FLOP-poor CPU. They would raise $/M by 1.9-3.5× compared with the same backbone run autoregressively, and they lose 5-9 points of quality.

findings.claim: Phi family. Phi-4 14B (Dec 2024, MIT, 16k context): MMLU-Pro 70.4, GPQA 56.1, IFEval 63.0. Phi-4-mini 3.8B: MMLU ~67, GSM8K ~88. Phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning uses the SambaY hybrid and is a math-reasoning specialist. Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B came out in March 2026. Claims of a 'Phi-5' (14B dense) appear only on third-party hosting blogs; I found no Microsoft announcement.
findings.relevance: Phi-4, the user's suggestion, is dominated. It is estimated at ~$1.7/M because 14B dense still costs 27 GFLOP/token, which is more than Qwen3.5-9B, and it is 12-25 points lower on MMLU-Pro, GPQA and IFEval. Its 16k context and weak instruction following hurt extraction work.

findings.claim: gpt-oss-20b: 21B total, 3.6B active, 24 layers, 32 experts with top-4, hidden 2880, alternating 128-token sliding-window and full attention, 201k vocab. Experts are MXFP4 (14 GB) and are dequantized to BF16 where MXFP4 isn't native, which likely includes vLLM CPU (~42 GB). It scores MMLU 85.3 and GPQA 71.5 at high reasoning effort, but only 56.8 GPQA at low effort. It always emits a reasoning (analysis) channel, and its license is Apache 2.0.
findings.relevance: The estimate is $1.0-1.65/M per generated token at BF16. But its reasoning tokens inflate output by ~1.5-3× for a 128-token answer, and its quality at low effort is far below Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Low priority.

findings.claim: Other candidates, all dominated on quality, fit or CPU support. Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B: 31.6B total, ~3.2-3.6B active, 23 Mamba-2 + 6 GQA layers with MoE (128 experts top-6 + 2 shared), MMLU-Pro 78.3, GPQA 73.0, NVIDIA Open Model License, CPU support unverified. Granite 4.1 dense 3B/8B/30B (Apache 2.0): MMLU-Pro 49.8/56.0/64.1, IFEval 82.3/87.1/89.7. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B: MMLU-Pro 55.5. LFM2-8B-A1B: MMLU-Pro 37.4, GPQA 29.3. LFM2-24B-A2B: GPQA 47.4. Mistral Small 4 (119B-A6.5B, Apache 2.0): MMLU-Pro 78.0, GPQA 71.2, but decode would read ~60-119 GB per step. ERNIE-4.5-21B-A3B: snippet values (MMLU-Pro 77.6, GPQA 81.1) are unverified.
findings.relevance: None beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B or Qwen3.5-9B on quality at a similar or lower CPU cost, so none should take VM time now.

findings.claim: SGLang's native Xeon/AMX backend has BF16, INT8 and FP8 kernels for dense and MoE FFNs, reports ~85% memory-bandwidth efficiency for INT8 MoE, and claims 6-14× TTFT and 2-4× TPOT vs llama.cpp. It lists Qwen3 MoE among optimized models. Whether it supports Qwen3.5/3.6 GDN on CPU is unconfirmed. vLLM's VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL flag reuses these kernels, but only for BF16 weights.
findings.relevance: If vLLM's default CPU MoE path turns out slow for prefill, try VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1 with BF16 weights first, then SGLang CPU (E14).

findings.claim: 4-bit quantization of Qwen3.8-27B keeps ~97% of FP16 accuracy (Q4_K_M/AWQ across 800 agentic tasks, Terminal-Bench parity), and quality drops off below 2 bits.
findings.relevance: Quality is not the reason to avoid INT4. vLLM CPU's slow W4A16 kernels are (32 tok/s prefill in E17). For the candidates, INT8 or FP8 is the sweet spot on this stack.

ideas.idea: E19: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on vLLM 0.31.0 CPU (same image and vllm_bench.sh as E17). Order: official BF16 with default MoE prepack, then VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1, then official FP8 (W8A16 path) if it loads. Runs: prefill-only 512/1, decode 32/256 and mixed 512/128 at n=64/128/256, max-num-batched-tokens 8192-16384, KV space 24-32 GiB, enable_thinking=False, plus a 3-prompt correctness check.
ideas.hypothesis: BF16 mixed 512/128 at n=128 reaches ≥250 tok/s total (central estimate 330) and prefill ≥500 tok/s (central 750). FP8/INT8 at n=128 reaches ≥400 tok/s (central 400-510). This is falsified if BF16 mixed throughput is below 180 tok/s, which would mean CPU MoE kernel efficiency < 0.2.
ideas.expected_gain: From $3.47/M (27B W8A8, n=64, measured) to ~$1.42/M BF16 (range $1.20-1.70; 1.681×1.70 s/3600/640) and ~$0.92/M INT8 (range $0.76-1.11). That is a 2.4-4.5× reduction. Even at MoE prefill efficiency 0.2 it is $1.47/M. Spot-equivalent ≈ $0.18-0.27/M.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~2.5 VM-hours (~$4.2) on one E16ds_v7. Downloads are 67 GB BF16 + 35 GB FP8 at ~1 GB/s (<3 min). Model load takes ~5 min per configuration. Risks: the qwen3_5_moe CPU path may fail on 0.31 (the recipe says vLLM ≥0.17 on Xeon 6), FP8 W8A16 MoE may be absent on CPU, and BF16 weights (70 GB) plus 32 GiB KV leave ~20 GB headroom on 128 GiB.
ideas.prerequisites: Reuse the bench/vllm_chain.sh profile with a model list. GDN state is ~63 MB/seq, so n=256 needs ~16 GB of state plus ~3 GB KV. Record the image digest and model revisions. Save results after every step (watchdog rule).

ideas.idea: E19b: Qwen3.5-9B dense hybrid on vLLM CPU as a low-risk dense control: BF16, plus a self-made INT8 W8A8 (llm-compressor round-to-nearest, per-channel weights, dynamic per-token activations, ignore lm_head; no calibration data needed; run on the VM), n=64/128/256.
ideas.hypothesis: BF16 mixed 512/128 at n=128 reaches ≥250 tok/s (central 306), and W8A8 reaches ≥380 tok/s (central 444). Prefill reaches ≥360 tok/s at BF16 and ≥540 at W8A8, i.e. ~3.4-3.9× the 27B, because it does 13.8 vs 54 GFLOP/token.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-hours (~$2.5). The 19 GB download is trivial. It uses the exact qwen3_5 code path that already works for the 27B, so setup risk is very low. llm-compressor must be pip-installed inside the VM (VM internet is fine).
ideas.prerequisites: Run on the same VM as E19 so the comparison is like-for-like (E08 found 9-25% variance between instances). Check that a W8A8 run from vLLM is coherent before benchmarking it.

ideas.idea: E20: quality gate in non-thinking mode for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-9B vs the Qwen3.8-27B W8A8 E16 results. Use the E16 harness (GSM8K, MMLU subset), add IFEval (strict prompt-level), a JSON field-extraction set (exact-match F1 and schema validity) and a classification set (e.g. Banking77 or AG News accuracy). Optionally add a summarization faithfulness check judged offline by Qwen3.8-27B.
ideas.hypothesis: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B lands within 2 points of the 27B on MMLU/GSM8K and within 3 points on IFEval strict. Qwen3.5-9B lands within 4-5 points. Both reach ≥98% JSON schema validity with guided decoding. The 27B's advantage is largest on strict-format and multi-constraint instructions, consistent with Qwen3.8's +10 IFBench over 3.6.
ideas.expected_gain: It decides whether the 2.4-4.5× cost reduction can be taken. It does not change throughput.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1-1.5 VM-hours per model on CPU, and it can run in the same chain after E19/E19b. Subsets of ~300-500 items per benchmark at ~300-500 tok/s take ~20-40 min each.
ideas.prerequisites: E16 results for Qwen3.8-27B W8A8/BF16 as the reference. Datasets downloaded on the VM (HF is reachable from the VM). Fixed prompts and greedy decoding. Pass enable_thinking=False through chat_template_kwargs.

ideas.idea: E21: Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it on vLLM CPU, BF16, n=64/128/256 mixed/prefill/decode, as a cross-family hedge and the autoregressive control for DiffusionGemma.
ideas.hypothesis: BF16 mixed 512/128 at n=128 reaches ≥270 tok/s (central 342), and prefill ≥450 tok/s. It fails to load if the CPU fused-MoE GELU_TANH gap (vLLM #43326) is still present in 0.31.
ideas.expected_gain: $1.36/M BF16 (range $1.11-1.69) and ~$0.89/M INT8 if a W8A8 build exists, vs $3.47/M. Quality is ~3 points below Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on MMLU-Pro and GPQA.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-hours (~$2.5). Download ~52 GB.
ideas.prerequisites: Only worth running if E19 shows vLLM CPU MoE works, or if Qwen MoE fails for a Qwen-specific reason. Check the vLLM 0.31 cpu_moe activation list first.

ideas.idea: MoE tuning inside E19: raise max-num-batched-tokens (2048 → 8192 → 16384) so each expert receives more tokens per prefill GEMM. Compare VLLM_CPU_MOE_PREPACK=1 vs 0 vs VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1. Log the distinct experts touched per decode step to validate f(n).
ideas.hypothesis: Prefill tok/s for the MoE rises ≥30% from 2048 to 16384 batched tokens. The per-expert token count M goes from ~64 to ~512, which moves AMX GEMMs from overhead-bound to compute-bound. The 27B's prefill did not scale this way.
ideas.expected_gain: Prefill is ~35-45% of the MoE request time, so +30% prefill gives roughly −10% $/M (e.g. $0.92 → $0.83/M INT8).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.5 VM-hour on top of E19.
ideas.prerequisites: E19 BF16 run working.

ideas.idea: DiffusionGemma CPU sanity check, only to close the user's question with data. Run DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B-it BF16 via HF Transformers ≥5.11 (or vLLM CPU if Model Runner V2 runs on CPU), measuring seconds per 256-token denoising step and steps per answer at batch 1, 4 and 16 on 512-token prompts with 128-token answers. Compare with Gemma 4 26B-A4B AR from E21 on the same VM.
ideas.hypothesis: The $/M for a 512/128 workload is ≥1.9× worse than AR Gemma 4 at n≥64 (central ~3×). A step costs ≈256 × the per-token prefill cost, and ~12-14 steps are needed per block.
ideas.expected_gain: None expected (negative result): estimated $2.7-3.9/M vs $0.9-1.4/M for AR, and it would document why diffusion LMs don't help offline CPU batch work.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-hour (~$1.7). Risks: Transformers' diffusion generate on CPU may be very slow or single-request, the vLLM CPU backend may not support Model Runner V2, and llama.cpp support is an unmerged PR with no batching.
ideas.prerequisites: E21 done (for the AR control on the same VM). Run only if the user wants empirical confirmation.

ideas.idea: Watch list, no VM time now. (a) Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (6B active, GPQA 91.7) on an E20ds_v7 (160 GiB, 20 vCPU = full regional family quota, $2.079/h) once mainline llama.cpp or vLLM CPU supports it and a ≤110 GB 4-6-bit build exists. (b) A future Qwen3.8 ~35B-A3B, if Qwen releases one (community request #120). (c) gpt-oss-20b and Nemotron 3 Nano only if every Qwen/Gemma MoE run fails.
