Stack-agnostic throughput optimization f.topic: Stack-agnostic throughput optimization for offline CPU batch inference of Qwen3.8-27B on Azure Xeon AMX (E16ds_v6/v7), including diffusion LLMs (DiffusionGemma)
Stack-agnostic throughput optimization f.summary: Baseline update: the task text's $4.56/M is out of date. Round 2 already brought the best cost down to $2.39/M on E16ds_v6 (E18) and $3.47/M on E16ds_v7 (E17), both W8A8 with 64 prompts. Per request on v6, prefill takes about 45% of the time (512/263 tok/s = 1.95 s) and decode about 55% (128/54.3 = 2.36 s). Decode at 64 sequences runs at the same speed on v6 and v7 (54.3 vs 55.2 tok/s), even though their prefill differs by 34%. So the decode step (~1.18 s, about 0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence) is limited by per-sequence work, not by DRAM bandwidth or prefill-style GEMM speed. The vLLM logs show one cause: Qwen3.8 keeps its Gated DeltaNet state in FP32 (154 MB per sequence), so 64 sequences read and write ~20 GB of state per decode step. The same FP32 state makes vLLM use an 896-token attention block. Prefix caching works per block, so the reference 512-token prompts get 0% prefix-cache hits however much of the instruction they share. Prefix caching only pays for shared prefixes of 896 tokens or more, or with the fine-grained mode, which requires MTP. Three P0 tests remain cheap and likely to pay: (1) 128–256 sequences with the KV cache sized to fit (−7 to −13%), (2) BF16 state via --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype (−4 to −8%, twice as many sequences per GiB, half the block size; needs an accuracy check), (3) a shared-prefix matrix (0% for the reference workload, −35 to −50% per request when instructions are long). MTP k=1 is already measured at +16% decode on real text (−7% blended). Workload shaping matters as much: thinking is on by default in Qwen3.8 and must be turned off, and halving output length cuts $/request by ~27% (~19% per million tokens). FP8 KV cache, FP8 compute (no AMX-FP8 before Diamond Rapids), W4A8, activation sparsity and runtime/Linux knobs are each worth about 0–5% here. Diffusion LLMs don't fit this job. DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B needs ~130–270 GFLOP per useful output token, against 54 for Qwen3.8 autoregressive decoding. Its quality is below its autoregressive sibling Gemma 4 26B-A4B, its vLLM Xeon recipe runs only 4 sequences at a time, and the literature finds autoregressive models win on throughput at large batch. If that family is tested at all, the autoregressive Gemma 4 26B-A4B (R04) is the candidate, at an estimated $0.75–1.7/M. Realistic targets: ~$1.9–2.0/M for the 512/128 reference on v6 (decode ×1.4 from batch + BF16 state + MTP), and ~$1.2–1.6/M for jobs with long shared prefixes or short outputs. WebFetch was blocked for every external host, so web claims come from search-result snippets; repository numbers come from the E16, E17 and E18 raw logs.

findings.claim: Current best measured cost is $2.39/M blended (512/128) on E16ds_v6 with vLLM 0.31 W8A8 at 64 prompts (prefill 263 tok/s, decode 54.3 out tok/s, mixed 154.1 total tok/s); E16ds_v7 gives $3.47/M on a slower instance. Per request (64 in flight): prefill 512/263=1.95 s (45%), decode 128/54.3=2.36 s (55%), measured 4.15 s. Decode at 64 sequences is identical on v6 and v7 (54.3 vs 55.2 tok/s) while prefill differs 34% and llama.cpp decode differs 13%, so the decode step is not DRAM- or GEMM-throughput-bound.
findings.relevance: Defines the baseline and shows decode (55% of time) is the bigger lever; any technique must be judged against this split.

findings.claim: Decode step time fits ~0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence (v6: 0.511 s at 16 seqs, 1.179 s at 64; v7: 0.593/0.724/1.159 s at 16/32/64). Extrapolation: ~62 out tok/s at 128 seqs (+14%), ~67 at 256 (+22%), with a ceiling of ~72 tok/s. Only ~0.3 s per step is weight streaming (~30 GB at ~90 GB/s); the ~14 ms per-sequence cost is the floor.
findings.relevance: Bounds what larger batches, MTP and weight compression can do: weight-byte reductions (W4A8) hit only the ~0.3 s fixed part, per-sequence work dominates.

findings.claim: The Gated DeltaNet SSM state is FP32. Qwen3.5/3.8 configs set mamba_ssm_dtype=float32 and vLLM reads it. The logs confirm it: 'Setting attention block size to 896 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size' and 'Padding mamba page size by 14.43%', which matches 48 V-heads x 128 x 128 x 4 B = 3.15 MB + 61 KB conv state per layer. That is ~154 MB per sequence over 48 layers, and ~9.9 GB of state at 64 sequences, read and written every decode step (~20 GB of traffic, ~0.2-0.3 s of the 1.18 s step). vLLM exposes --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype; Qwen guidance says quality may suffer below FP32.
findings.relevance: BF16 state would remove ~10 GB/step at 64 seqs (decode +9-16%), double sequences per KV GiB, and halve the hybrid block size (896 -> ~400-416), which changes when prefix caching can hit.

findings.claim: In vLLM, prefix caching for hybrid GDN models works at block granularity. With 896-token blocks on our CPU (528 on GPU, issue #40696), prompts or shared prefixes shorter than one block get 0% hits. In the default 'align' mamba cache mode only the checkpoint at the last block boundary before the prompt end is kept, so hits drop to 0% when that boundary falls in request-unique tokens (#45238). Partial/fine-grained hits exist (--enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache, PR #46384), but only with align mode, EAGLE/MTP speculation on the Mamba group, and a prefix-match unit smaller than the block. Some sources say GDN does not support 'all' mode; PR #36649 adds it for Qwen3.5/Qwen3Next. vLLM 0.31 CPU enables prefix caching by default (enable_prefix_caching=True in our logs).
findings.relevance: The R03 hypothesis (400 shared tokens of 512 -> 4x cheaper prefill) cannot work with defaults: our 512-token reference prompts get no hits. Prefix caching pays only for shared prefixes >= 896 tokens (or ~416 with BF16 state), or with fine-grained mode plus MTP.

findings.claim: MTP on real text (GSM8K, W8A8, 64 sequences, v6): k=1 gives +16% output tok/s at 95.9% acceptance, k=2 +14%, k=3 +6%, accuracy unchanged. With random prompts it loses 28-44%. MTP reduces KV capacity: 24 GiB holds 99,669 tokens without MTP, 70,485 with k=1, 56,388 with k=2. Known vLLM issues: CPU GDN + MTP + structured output can kill the EngineCore (#56419, fix PR #56518); MTP prefix-cache correctness on hybrid models (#47861, #53504).
findings.relevance: MTP k=1 is a measured ~-7% blended win (55% decode share x 1-1/1.16). It competes with batch size for KV memory and is a prerequisite for fine-grained hybrid prefix caching.

findings.claim: Speculative decoding at high batch: verification is compute-bound and gains shrink as batch grows. MagicDec gets speedups at batch 32-256 only for long contexts where KV reads dominate; ours are short. SuffixDecoding (Arctic Inference plugin, vLLM speculative method 'suffix') matches prompt and previous outputs with a suffix tree at ~20 us per speculated token on CPU. It adapts how far it speculates and reports 5.3x on AgenticSQL and 2.5x on SWE-Bench (6.3-7.8 accepted tokens per step) at low batch. vLLM also has 'ngram' prompt lookup.
findings.relevance: At ~14 ms per sequence per step, each verified draft token costs about a full token of GEMM plus state work. Model-free speculation pays only on copy-heavy extraction where acceptance is very high (expected 0-40% decode).

findings.claim: The KV cache is a small share of memory and traffic for this hybrid. 16 full-attention layers x 4 KV heads x 256 dims x 2 B = 64 KB/token, i.e. ~42 MB per 640-token sequence vs 154 MB of GDN state, and ~2% of decode-step traffic. vLLM's CPU backend supports only fp8_e5m2 KV (e4m3 is cast), historically not with chunked prefill or prefix caching. A vLLM RFC notes FP8 KV gives little to no memory benefit on Mamba/GDN hybrids, because the unified page size follows the state.
findings.relevance: FP8/INT8 KV-cache quantization is ~0% for our $/M; the state dtype is the memory/traffic lever, not the KV dtype.

findings.claim: No native FP8 compute on Granite or Emerald Rapids: Granite Rapids adds AMX-FP16 and AMX-COMPLEX, while AMX-FP8 and AVX10.2 arrive with Diamond Rapids (now reported for 2027). vLLM does have CPUFp8BlockScaledMMKernel, an FP8 W8A16 block-quantized GEMM via AMX BRGEMM: activations stay BF16, K-block must be 128 and N-block a multiple of 32. Qwen's official Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 is block-wise [128,128] (28.3 GB), reported near-identical to BF16. SGLang's CPU backend likewise emulates FP8 on top of BF16 AMX.
findings.relevance: FP8 cannot beat W8A8 on cost: prefill runs at BF16 AMX speed (E09 BF16 133 vs W8A8 198 tok/s), though decode bytes match INT8. It is a quality-preserving option given W8A8's measured -2.75 MMLU points (E16).

findings.claim: INT4 paths on x86 vLLM are slow for this model: compressed-tensors W4A16 is 5-8x slower in prefill and 2.3x slower in decode than W8A8 (E17/E18). vLLM's CPU W4A8 (INT4 weights, INT8 compute) is implemented for MoE experts (fused_experts_cpu INT4_W4A8), not documented for dense linear layers. torchao's DA8W4 (Int8DynamicActivationInt4WeightConfig, AMX through Inductor max-autotune, PyTorch 2.8) is reported on par with vLLM offline on Llama-3.1-8B. Because decode at 64 sequences is not weight-bandwidth-bound, halving weight bytes would help only the ~0.3 s fixed part of the step.
findings.relevance: W4A8 or per-group INT4 with INT8 compute is worth <=5% blended at batch 64, against a large engineering and quality cost. W8A8 stays the format.

findings.claim: Activation sparsity does not survive batching. TEAL's authors state speedups decrease as batch grows and their sparsity does not scale to higher batch sizes. Deja Vu's union of active MLP neurons rises from <1% at batch 1 to ~75% at batch 32. SparAMX (AMX + unstructured weight sparsity) reports 1.42x end-to-end on Llama-3-8B, mainly at low batch, and needs pruned weights.
findings.relevance: ~0% at our 64-256-sequence decode (SwiGLU, not ReLU, adds to it); not worth VM time.

findings.claim: vLLM 0.31 CPU defaults, from our logs and docs: chunked prefill on with max_num_batched_tokens=4096 (the documented offline default), prefix caching on, torch.compile mode DYNAMO_TRACE_ONCE. The AOT compile cache fails to load ('function' object has no attribute 'finalize_loading'), so each engine start recompiles (~2.5-3 min). Async scheduling is forcibly disabled on the CPU platform. The vllm-openai-cpu Dockerfile already sets LD_PRELOAD to tcmalloc and libiomp5. VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL (AMX small-batch kernels) requires BF16 weights. Docs recommend one OpenMP thread per physical core; E17 measured −51% with 16 threads.
findings.relevance: R06's tcmalloc/Intel OpenMP gains are probably already in the image (verify with one env dump). The remaining knobs (THP, larger chunk budget, compile-cache fix) are worth single-digit percent or startup time only.

findings.claim: Transparent huge pages give small, mixed effects. Phoronix on Linux 6.18 (llama.cpp CPU) found 'always' faster for text generation at batch 128 but 'madvise' faster for prompt processing. AMD's ZenDNN guide recommends madvise for LLMs; typical gains are 0-3% (~10% at best).
findings.relevance: Worth adding to a knob bundle (0-5%), not its own VM run; CPU governor and SNC aren't controllable on Azure (the VM is 1 NUMA node, turbo already active).

findings.claim: Workload shaping: Qwen3.8-27B thinks by default; chat_template_kwargs {enable_thinking: false} disables it (E16 ran that way). LLMLingua-2, a token classifier on XLM-RoBERTa-large (~0.56B), compresses prompts 2-5x with 1.6-2.9x end-to-end latency gains. XGrammar is the fastest structured-output engine, but grammar processing is CPU-side work whose cost grows with batch. On our VM it would share the 8 cores with the OpenMP threads; SMT contention already halved throughput in E17.
findings.relevance: Output tokens cost ~5x input tokens here ($6.78 vs $1.40/M on v6). Halving output cuts $/request ~27%, and leaving thinking on can multiply cost per request 3-10x.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma (Google DeepMind, 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is built on Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE (25.2B total, ~3.8B active, 128 experts with 8 active, 262k vocab). It denoises a 256-token canvas with up to 48 steps, adaptive stopping ~12-16 steps, ~15-20 tokens finalized per pass. Quality is below Gemma 4 AR: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, MMMLU 81.5 vs 86.3, GSM8K 96.3 vs 96.7, LiveCodeBench 1429 vs 1718. vLLM supports it natively; its recipe covers Xeon 6 with the vllm-openai-cpu image at --max-num-seqs 4 and mentions >=4 NUMA nodes. The cap comes from diffusion state buffers of max_seqs x canvas x vocab; Red Hat runs it as a small-canvas 'decision' classifier at max-num-seqs 8. GGUF/llama.cpp also run it. The 1,000+ tok/s figure is batch 1 on H100; sources say parallel decoding gives diminishing returns when servers batch many requests.
findings.relevance: This is the diffusion candidate the user asked about. Its strengths are latency at low batch and a small active parameter count; our goal is batch throughput on compute-bound CPUs.

findings.claim: Diffusion LMs lose on throughput at batch. 'How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models?' finds LLaMA3-8B-Instruct 13.7x the throughput of LLaDA-8B: DLMs are compute-bound with more FLOPs per token, and their accelerations (dual cache, parallel decoding) help mainly at small batch. Fast-dLLM likewise reports AR overtaking prefix-cached dLLMs as batch grows. Our arithmetic for DiffusionGemma at ~15 passes x 256 positions x (7.6 GFLOP body + ~1.1-1.5 GFLOP logits): ~130 GFLOP per output token with a full canvas, ~270 when only 128 of 256 positions are used. That compares with 54 GFLOP for Qwen3.8-27B AR and ~7.6 for Gemma 4 26B-A4B AR. Diffusion drafters (SpecDiff-2, up to 5.5x) target the same low-batch regime.
findings.relevance: On our CPU, already compute/per-row-bound at batch 64, DiffusionGemma's decode would reach ~13-50 out tok/s against Qwen W8A8's 54. Its only advantage is MoE prefill, which the same family's autoregressive Gemma 4 26B-A4B also has, with far cheaper decode.

findings.claim: The 64-prompt benchmark runs carry ~8-9 s of fixed per-run overhead. On v6, marginal prefill between 16 and 64 prompts is 283 tok/s vs 263 measured. vllm bench throughput supports shared-prefix workloads (--random-prefix-len; the prefix_repetition dataset with prefix-len, suffix-len, num-prefixes and output-len).
findings.relevance: Long production jobs should be ~3-7% cheaper than the reported 64-prompt numbers. Prefix-caching tests need no custom client.

ideas.idea: P0-A: Larger batches at steady state. W8A8 on E16ds_v6, mixed 512/128 with num_prompts at least 4x max_num_seqs, max_num_seqs 64/128/192 (256 if memory allows), VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE 24/40/60 GiB (each sequence of <=896 tokens takes one 896-token block in every layer, ~235 MB with FP32 state). Record a llama-bench reference on the same VM and log vLLM's KV concurrency line.
ideas.hypothesis: Decode step ~0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence, so out tok/s rises 54 -> ~62 at 128 (+14%) and ~67 at 256 (+22%), with prefill flat; long runs also amortize the ~9 s per-run overhead. Falsified if 128 sequences give <+5% decode, or if preemptions show the KV cache is too small.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode time per request 2.36 -> 2.07 s (128) or 1.92 s (256); per request 4.31 -> 4.02/3.87 s = -7%/-10%, about -3% more from steady state. $2.39 -> ~$2.15-2.22/M on v6 ($3.47 -> ~$3.1-3.2 on v7). Measured from the task's $4.56 reference, 16->64 prompts plus v6 have already given -48%.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h on E16ds_v6 (~$2): three 25-35 min runs plus ~15 min setup. RSS must stay below ~115 GB with 60 GiB KV, so step 64 -> 128 -> 192 and stop on OOM.
ideas.prerequisites: vllm_bench.sh needs MAX_NUM_SEQS and NUM_PROMPTS knobs; current image digest 8024248339dc. A real-text variant is needed if MTP is combined (see P1-D).

ideas.idea: P0-B: BF16 GDN state (--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16) with W8A8. Measure decode at 64 and 128 sequences and mixed 512/128, then GSM8K-200 and MMLU-400 agreement against FP32-state W8A8 (E16 scripts).
ideas.hypothesis: FP32 state is ~154 MB per sequence (~20 GB read+write per decode step at 64 sequences). BF16 halves it: decode +9-16%, hybrid block size 896 -> ~400-416 tokens (check the log line), and 2x sequences per KV GiB. Answer agreement with the FP32-state run >=97% on GSM8K and MMLU at <=1k-token contexts. Falsified if decode gains <4%, vLLM ignores the override for Qwen3.8's config, or MMLU drops >1 point.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode 2.36 -> ~2.10 s per request, blended -4% to -8%: $2.39 -> ~$2.2-2.3/M. Combined with P0-A it lets 256 sequences fit in ~30 GiB instead of ~60. The ~416-token block also enables prefix hits for 512-token prompts that share >=416 tokens (see P0-C).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h (throughput 0.5 h; quality ~25 min for GSM8K+MMLU with W8A8; setup). Risk: the CPU GDN kernel may not accept a BF16 state, and Qwen ships FP32 for a reason.
ideas.prerequisites: Confirm the flag exists in vLLM 0.31 (vllm serve --help in the container); reuse bench/quality_tasks.py.

ideas.idea: P0-C: Shared-prefix matrix with prefix caching. vllm bench throughput --dataset-name prefix_repetition (one prefix), W8A8, 128 sequences. Cases: (a) 384 shared + 128 unique, 128 out, defaults (expect 0% hits); (b) 896 shared + 384 unique, 128 out (expect a hit at the 896 boundary); (c) case (a) with MTP k=1 + --mamba-cache-mode align + --enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache + a small prefix-match unit; (d) case (a) with BF16 state (block ~416). Each against --no-enable-prefix-caching, logging the prefix-cache hit rate and spot-checking outputs for correctness.
ideas.hypothesis: With FP32 state, prefix caching only hits for shared prefixes >=896 tokens whose last block boundary falls inside the shared part. Fine-grained mode or BF16 state brings 384-416-token shared prefixes into reach. Falsified if (b) shows <50% of the predicted prefill saving, or if (c) and (d) show 0% hits.
ideas.expected_gain: (a): 0 for the reference workload. (b): per request 1280/263+2.36 = 7.23 s -> 384/263+2.36 = 3.82 s, i.e. -47%. If (c) or (d) works for 384-of-512 shared: 4.31 -> 2.85 s, i.e. -34%, $2.39 -> ~$1.58/M with cached input tokens counted. That is the biggest lever for real batch jobs with long common instructions. Padding instructions to a block boundary, e.g. with few-shot examples, costs nothing once cached.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h. Risk: fine-grained flags may postdate 0.31 or be GPU-only; hybrid prefix caching plus MTP has had correctness bugs (#47861, #53504, #57267).
ideas.prerequisites: Verify flag names in the 0.31 image. Ask the user for realistic shared-prefix and unique lengths of target jobs.

ideas.idea: P1-D: MTP k=1 combined with larger batches on real 512/128 text, e.g. 512-token news articles summarized in <=128 tokens with thinking off. Configurations: 64 and 128 sequences, MTP 0/1, KV sized for MTP's ~29% lower capacity (24 GiB holds 70,485 tokens with MTP vs 99,669 without).
ideas.hypothesis: MTP's +16% decode at 64 sequences (GSM8K, 96% acceptance) carries over to summarization/extraction text with >=85% acceptance, and stays >= +10% at 128 sequences. Falsified if gains at 128 drop below +5% (per-sequence verification cost dominates).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h; needs a real dataset downloaded on the VM (Hugging Face from the VM is fine).
ideas.prerequisites: Fix for CPU GDN+MTP+structured-output crash (#56419/#56518) if structured output will be used; P0-A results to pick KV size.

ideas.idea: P1-E: Profile one decode step at 64 sequences (W8A8, decode 32/256): torch profiler or perf plus py-spy. Attribute the ~1.18 s step to GEMMs at M=64, GDN recurrent kernel and state copies, attention, sampler (64 x 248k logits), RMSNorm/conv and Python scheduling.
ideas.hypothesis: Of the ~14 ms per-sequence cost, roughly 4-6 ms is GEMM at decode-sized M, 3-5 ms the FP32 GDN state, and 3-5 ms other work (sampler RNG over 16M logits, Python), because decode speed doesn't change with instance speed. Falsified if GEMM is >70% of the step.
ideas.expected_gain: No direct gain. It decides between kernel work (SGLang, R02/E14), state dtype (P0-B) and batch size (P0-A) for the 55% of time spent in decode. If ~4 ms of non-GEMM overhead per sequence could be removed, decode would gain ~+30%, about -15% blended.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.5 VM-h; it can run at the end of the P0-A chain.
ideas.prerequisites: perf in cloud-init (E07 used it); VLLM_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR or perf record on the EngineCore PID.

ideas.idea: P1-F: Output budget and structured-output overhead. Same 512-token real inputs with (i) free text, max_tokens 128; (ii) JSON schema via xgrammar with short keys; (iii) a terse prompt. Measure output tokens per request, wall time, and grammar overhead at 64-128 sequences. Confirm enable_thinking=false is the default in every bench script.
ideas.hypothesis: JSON or terse output halves output tokens (128 -> ~64) at equal task quality, and xgrammar adds <5% per step even though it shares cores with the OpenMP threads. Falsified if the grammar costs >10% of throughput or MTP+grammar crashes.
ideas.expected_gain: Per request 1.95 + 1.18 = 3.13 s vs 4.31 s: $/request -27%, $/M on 576 tokens -19% ($2.39 -> ~$1.93/M). Leaving thinking on (~+1000 output tokens) would cost ~5x per request.
ideas.prerequisites: A labelled extraction or classification sample to check that output-length cuts don't hurt quality.

ideas.idea: P2-G: Model-free speculation for copy-heavy extraction: vLLM 'ngram' (prompt lookup) and 'suffix' (Arctic Inference) at 64 sequences on an extraction task whose outputs quote input spans.
ideas.hypothesis: On copy-heavy outputs, suffix decoding gets >=2 accepted tokens per step and speculates adaptively, so decode gains +15-40% at 64 sequences. On free-form text the gain is ~0 or negative. Falsified if acceptance stays below ~1 token per step, or the hybrid GDN model rejects non-MTP drafters.
ideas.expected_gain: 0 to -16% blended for extraction jobs (0.55 x 0..0.29). Likely smaller than MTP on general text, and they can't be stacked.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h. Risk: arctic-inference must pip-install into the vLLM 0.31 CPU image and support it; hybrid state rollback for these methods is unverified.
ideas.prerequisites: A representative extraction dataset; pip on the VM.

ideas.idea: P2-H: Runtime knob bundle in one chain: THP=always (set before the model loads, defrag defer+madvise); --no-enable-prefix-caching when nothing is shared; max_num_batched_tokens 8192/16384; check LD_PRELOAD inside the image (tcmalloc + libiomp5); compile-cache workaround (VLLM_USE_AOT_COMPILE=0 or a matching torch) to avoid the ~2.5-3 min recompile on each start.
ideas.hypothesis: Each knob is worth 0-5% of steady-state throughput and THP is the most likely to show. The cache fix saves ~2.5-3 min of startup per engine start. Falsified if every knob stays within run-to-run noise (~2%).
ideas.expected_gain: 0 to -8% blended combined (~$2.2-2.39/M), plus ~$0.06 per engine start; matters only for many short jobs.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.7 VM-h; fits at the tail of the P0 chain.
ideas.prerequisites: --privileged container (already used); root access to /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage on the VM.

ideas.idea: P2-I: Official Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (block 128x128) through vLLM's CPUFp8BlockScaledMMKernel (FP8 W8A16, AMX-BF16 BRGEMM) as a quality-safe alternative to community W8A8.
ideas.hypothesis: It loads on CPU, prefill runs at ~BF16 speed (~0.7x W8A8), decode at 64 sequences lands between BF16 and W8A8, and MMLU stays within 1 point of BF16 (W8A8 lost 2.75 points, p=0.035).
ideas.expected_gain: Cost goes up about 20-40% compared with W8A8 (~$2.9-3.3/M on v6), but likely BF16-level accuracy at ~25% below BF16 cost. Use it only where W8A8's MMLU-type loss is unacceptable.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h (throughput plus MMLU-400/GSM8K-200).
ideas.prerequisites: Hugging Face download on the VM; confirm the kernel exists in vLLM 0.31.

ideas.idea: P2-J: LLMLingua-2 prompt compression (xlm-roberta-large) at 2x before vLLM, on a labelled extraction or classification set.
ideas.hypothesis: 2x compression of the unique part of the prompt keeps task accuracy within 1-2 points for classification, less reliably for extraction of exact spans; compressor cost is ~1-2% of the 27B prefill.
ideas.expected_gain: Prefill 1.95 -> ~1.0 s + 0.05 s for compression, so per request -22%: $2.39 -> ~$1.86 per original-token million. It overlaps with prefix caching (compress only the unique part).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h; quality risk dominates.
ideas.prerequisites: pip on the VM, a labelled dataset; job owner accepts lossy inputs.

ideas.idea: P3-K: Diffusion LLM check: DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B on vLLM CPU (BF16, recipe flags, max-num-seqs 4/8/16), next to its autoregressive sibling Gemma 4 26B-A4B as the control, on 512/128 and on a short-canvas classification task.
ideas.hypothesis: DiffusionGemma's decode needs ~130-270 GFLOP per useful output token against Qwen3.8 AR's 54. On a compute-bound 8-core VM it reaches only ~13-50 out tok/s; prefill (3.8B active) runs ~460-900 tok/s. Per request 0.6-1.1 s + 2.5-9.8 s = 3.1-10.9 s against Qwen W8A8's 4.15 s, so no reliable gain at lower quality. The AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B gets the same prefill plus ~70-180 tok/s decode at 64 sequences (~1.3-3.0 s per request). Falsified if DiffusionGemma beats the AR control per request at equal batch.
ideas.expected_gain: DiffusionGemma: -25% to +160% $/request vs the current $2.39/M (likely worse), with MMLU-Pro 5 points below Gemma 4. AR control: ~$0.75-1.7/M (-30 to -70%) at a quality cost to check like E16. That gain comes from the MoE model choice (R04), not from diffusion.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~2 VM-h for both models (downloads ~50 GB BF16 each). Risks: the recipe mentions >=4 NUMA nodes and max-num-seqs<=4, and diffusion state buffers are max_seqs x 256 x 262k.
ideas.prerequisites: Hugging Face access to google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it and Gemma 4 from the VM; E16-style quality harness adapted to Gemma chat templates.

ideas.idea: P3-L: Skip unless something changes: FP8/INT8 KV cache, W4A8 or DA8W4 dense kernels (torchao/SGLang), activation sparsity (TEAL/Deja Vu/SparAMX), EAGLE-3 heads, draft models.
ideas.hypothesis: Each is <=5% at batch 64-256 on this hybrid. KV is ~2% of decode traffic and gives no memory gain under hybrid page alignment. Decode isn't weight-bound. Union sparsity at batch >=32 is >=75% dense. The built-in MTP already accepts 96%.
ideas.expected_gain: ~0 to -5% blended each, for high engineering effort or quality risk.
ideas.cost_to_test: Not recommended; 1-3 VM-h each plus porting work.
ideas.prerequisites: Re-open only if P1-E's profile shows weight streaming dominating, or if batch can't grow.

open_questions: Does the vLLM 0.31.0 CPU image (digest 8024248339dc) honor --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16 for Qwen3.8, whose config pins float32, and does the CPU GDN kernel ('GDN decode kernel: CPU') support a BF16 state?

Are --enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache / partial hybrid prefix hits (PR #46384) and 'all' mamba cache mode (PR #36649) present in 0.31.0 and supported by the CPU attention backend? Exact flag names (prefix-match unit) need checking with --help.

What makes up the ~14 ms per-sequence decode cost at 64 sequences (decode-sized INT8 GEMMs, FP32 GDN state copies, sampler RNG over 64x248k logits, Python)? Decode doesn't change with instance speed (v6 54.3 vs v7 55.2 tok/s), so a profile is needed.

What do real target jobs look like (shared instruction length, unique input length, output length, copy-heavy extraction or not)? That decides whether prefix caching (needs >=896 shared tokens by default) and suffix decoding matter.
